# Process CDC dataframe - create numeric columns and generate state abbreviations
def processCDCDataFrame(df: pd.DataFrame):
    df['Percentage'] = pd.to_numeric(df.Percentage, errors='coerce')
    df['Lower Limit'] = pd.to_numeric(df['Lower Limit'], errors='coerce')
    df['Upper Limit'] = pd.to_numeric(df['Upper Limit'], errors='coerce')
    df['StateAbbr'] = df['State'].map(us_state_to_abbrev)
    return df


# Concat multiple dataframes with a column containing categories for each constituent dataframe
def joinDfs(dfs: list[pd.DataFrame], columnName: str, keys: list[str]):
    return pd.concat(dfs, keys=keys).reset_index(level=0, names=columnName).reset_index(drop=True)


# Loading raw CSV files
statesOverYearsDf = pd.read_csv('DiabetesAtlas_AllStatesLineChartData.csv')

stateEduAdult = pd.read_csv('DiabetesAtlas_States_Edu_Adult.csv')
stateEduHighSchool = pd.read_csv('DiabetesAtlas_States_Edu_HighSchool.csv')
stateEduKid = pd.read_csv('DiabetesAtlas_States_Edu_Kid.csv')

stateAgeYA = pd.read_csv('DiabetesAtlas_States_Age_YA.csv')
stateAgeAdult = pd.read_csv('DiabetesAtlas_States_Age_Adult.csv')
stateAgeRetiree = pd.read_csv('DiabetesAtlas_States_Age_Retirees.csv')
stateAgeElderly = pd.read_csv('DiabetesAtlas_States_Age_Elderly.csv')

# Processing raw CSV files and build final dataframe
statesOverYearsDf = processCDCDataFrame(statesOverYearsDf)

stateEduAdult = processCDCDataFrame(stateEduAdult)
stateEduHighSchool = processCDCDataFrame(stateEduHighSchool)
stateEduKid = processCDCDataFrame(stateEduKid)

stateAgeYA = processCDCDataFrame(stateAgeYA)
stateAgeAdult = processCDCDataFrame(stateAgeAdult)
stateAgeRetiree = processCDCDataFrame(stateAgeRetiree)
stateAgeElderly = processCDCDataFrame(stateAgeElderly)

stateAgeDf = joinDfs(
    [stateAgeYA, stateAgeAdult, stateAgeRetiree, stateAgeElderly],
    'AgeLevel',
    keys=['YA', 'Adult', 'Retirees', 'Elderly']
)

stateEduDf = joinDfs(
    [stateEduAdult, stateEduHighSchool, stateEduKid],
    'EducationLevel',
    keys=['Upper Level Study', 'High School Diploma', 'No High School']
)

# Distribtion of categorical variables
def describeCategorical(x: pd.Series):
    return pd.Series({
        'Missing Values': x.isna().sum(),
        'Unique Values': x.nunique(),
        'Top Levels': str(x.value_counts().nlargest(3).to_dict())
    })

2 Exploratory Data Analysis

2.1 Analysis 1 - The Current State of Diabetes in the US

By <Ash Dhamo>

Code 
# Calculate diabetes rate of change
statesOverYearsDf['PercentageDiff'] = statesOverYearsDf.groupby('StateAbbr')['Percentage'].diff()
stateEduDf['PercentageDiff'] = stateEduDf.groupby(['StateAbbr', 'EducationLevel'])['Percentage'].diff()
stateAgeDf['PercentageDiff'] = stateAgeDf.groupby(['StateAbbr', 'AgeLevel'])['Percentage'].diff()

To examine the current trends in diabetes rates across the US, we examined the prevalance of diabetes over a 22 year period, starting from 2000 up to the present day. We looked at the median number of diabetes cases between states across this time period. We also looked how quickly diabetes is increasing or decreasing in the country, as measured by the rate of change in the median diabetes cases. We observed that diabetes cases have continued to rise at a steady rate with no downturn in sight. While the rate of change has some seasonal variation across the time period, the average rate of change is around 0.18% per year, or around ~500k people per year newly diagnosed with diabetes.

Code 
g = sns.relplot(statesOverYearsDf[statesOverYearsDf.State == 'Median of States'],
                x='Year', y='Percentage',
                lw=4,

g.ax.set_title('US Median Diabetes Percentage')
g.set_xlabels('')
g.ax.set_ylim(4.5, 10)

plt.twinx()
ax = sns.lineplot(statesOverYearsDf[statesOverYearsDf.State == 'Median of States'],
                  x='Year', y='PercentageDiff',
                  lw=4, ls='--', color='orange')
ax.grid(False)
ax.set_ylabel("YoY Δ Percentage")
ax.set_ylim(-1, 3)
ax.tick_params(axis='y', length=0)

We also noticed that eight states had a high rate of change in diabetes, higher than our threshold of >0.25%. These states were “Alabama”, “Kentucky”, “Louisiana”, “Mississippi”, “New Mexico”, “Oklahoma”, “Virginia”, and “West Virginia”, the quickest growing regions in terms of diabetes prevalance.

Code 
# Calculate average rate of change, as well as states with an average rate of change > 0.25
meanStateDiff = statesOverYearsDf.groupby('StateAbbr')['PercentageDiff'].mean().reset_index()
meanMedianDiff = meanStateDiff[meanStateDiff.StateAbbr == 'MED']['PercentageDiff']
highStateDiff = meanStateDiff[meanStateDiff['PercentageDiff'] > 0.25].copy()
meanStateDiff.loc[meanStateDiff.StateAbbr == 'MED', 'StateAbbr'] = '~'

g = sns.catplot(meanStateDiff,
                x='StateAbbr', y='PercentageDiff', hue='PercentageDiff',
                aspect=3, legend_out=False)
g.set_xlabels('State')
g.set_ylabels('Average Yearly Change')

g.ax.plot('~', meanMedianDiff, 'o', markersize=12)
g.ax.text('~', meanMedianDiff + 0.01, 'Median', ha='center', va='bottom', weight='semibold')

g.ax.axhline(0.25, ls='-.')
g.ax.plot(highStateDiff.StateAbbr, highStateDiff.PercentageDiff, 'o', color='orange', markersize=10)
for i, row in highStateDiff.iterrows():
    g.ax.text(row['StateAbbr'], row['PercentageDiff'], f"  {row['StateAbbr']}",
              ha='left', va='center_baseline', color='black', weight='semibold')

g.ax.margins(x=0.01)
sns.move_legend(g.ax, 'center left', bbox_to_anchor=(1, 0.5), title='Δ Percentage')

2.2 Analysis 2: How might demographic factors contribute to complications and health outcomes of diabetes patients?

By <Sarah Huang>

To examine how demographic factors such as age, race, and gender may contribute to health outcomes and complications of diabetes patients, I first used a relevant subset of the dataset from diabetic patients in 130 hospitals from 1999 to 2008 that are related to demographic variables and potential outcomes. For demographic variables, I cleaned variables of gender and race by removing missing values because these values cannot be imputed. For outcomes, I mapped relevant discharge disposition IDs provided in a separate table. The rest of the discharge disposition IDs were not of interest and remained as NaN.

First, I considered the demographic variable of age, and its potential effects on outcomes such as number of medical diagnoses, the number of total procedures (lab and surgical procedures), and the time spent in the hospital for diabetic patients. I used catplots to show the relationship between categorical variables (a demographic variable) and a numerical variable (an outcome variable).

Code

As age increases, it was not unexpected to see that the number of medical diagnoses increased as well given that the body breaks down as we age.

Code

plot2.set_axis_labels("Age Groups", "Time in Hospital")
plot2.fig.suptitle("Time in Hospital by Age", y=1.05);

It was not unexpected to see the time in hospital increase as age also increased for similar reasons as to why number of medical diagnoses increased.

However, despite the number of medical diagnoses and time spent in the hospital increasing along with age, the number of total procedures by age does not change by any statistically significant amount, ranging from 41 to 45 procedures. For the elderly diabetic (considered in the age groups of [70-80), [80-90), and [90-100)), this suggests that despite having worse outcomes, the procedures are the same as other age groups and are not changing to adapt accordingly. This suggests the inefficient use of procedures for diabetic patients across age groups, therefore not optimally improving their health outcomes.

Next, I looked at how gender and racial group might affect outcomes for diabetic patients. I grouped the data by racial group and then assessed for the mean number of emergency visits per year by racial group. I then used catplot to graph the results in a barplot, using gender as the hue to see potential differences between gender.

Code

Next, I grouped number of emergencies by race. As mentioned previously, all racial groups have more emergency visits per year compared to Caucasians except diabetic Asians who are 50% less likely to go to the emergency room than Caucasians. I was curious to see if this meant that diabetic Asians had better outcomes than other racial groups, meausured by death and transfers to other facilities for continued care.

Code 
dischargedData = nomedData.copy().dropna()
#drop irrelevant mappings after we labeled relevant discharge outcomes (expired or transfers)

dischargedData['expired'] = dischargedData.discharge_disposition_id.str.contains('Expired').map(
    {True: 'Expired', False: 'Other Outcomes'})
#create a column that shows whether they expired or not

Based on the above graph and table, we can see that Asians have the highest proportion of transfers to a medical facility (0.72). 2.3 Analysis 3: How might prior medical care contribute to the outcomes of diabetes patients?

By <Eileen Wang>

To examine how prior medical care might contribute to the health outcomes of diabetes patients, I created a subset with relevant columns from the dataset from diabetic patients in 130 hospitals from 1999 to 2008 and focused on the admission source column. The admission source codes were organized into the following categories: physician referral, emergency room, hospital transfer, skilled nursing home transfer, and other healthcare facility transfer. Other admission source codes were not used as they either had no observations or did not constitute as prior medical care. I visualized the number of inpatient visits, number of total procedures, and time spent in hospital across these categories, using bar graphs. Number of total procedures was defined as the sum of both lab and other procedures.

Code 
# creating a subset from the dataset with relevant columns
nomedData1 = diabeticDataDf.loc[:, ['age', 'discharge_disposition_id', 'admission_source_id', 'number_inpatient',
                                    'time_in_hospital', 'num_lab_procedures', 'num_procedures',
                                    ]].copy()
Code 
nomedData1['num_total_procedures'] = nomedData1['num_procedures'] + nomedData1['num_lab_procedures']
Code 
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 5))

sns.barplot(data=nomedData1, x='admission_source_id', y='number_inpatient', ax=axes[0],
            palette=['#728FCE', '#9E7BFF', '#FC6C85', '#90EE90', '#F4A460'])
axes[0].set_xticklabels(axes[0].get_xticklabels(), rotation=50, ha='right')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Admission Source')
axes[0].set_ylabel('number_inpatient')

sns.barplot(data=nomedData1, x='admission_source_id', y='num_total_procedures',
            palette=['#728FCE', '#9E7BFF', '#FC6C85', '#90EE90', '#F4A460'], ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set_xticklabels(axes[1].get_xticklabels(), rotation=50, ha='right')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Admission Source')
axes[1].set_ylabel('num_total_procedures')

sns.barplot(data=nomedData1, x='admission_source_id', y='time_in_hospital',
            palette=['#728FCE', '#9E7BFF', '#FC6C85', '#90EE90', '#F4A460'], ax=axes[2])
axes[2].set_xticklabels(axes[2].get_xticklabels(), rotation=50, ha='right')
axes[2].set_xlabel('Admission Source')
axes[2].set_ylabel('time_in_hospital (day)')

plt.suptitle('Analysis by Admission Source')
plt.tight_layout()

From these graphs, you can see that patients from skilled nursing facilities consistently rank high across all three variables.

Across these admission sources, I also visualized the proportion of patient expiration in hospital, using a bar graph. Dummy variables were first created from the discharge disposition codes and new columns were made based on expiration codes. Expiration out of hospital was not analyzed as the causes of death could have been included other outside sources or confounding variables. Expiration in hospital was assumed to be the better indicator of health outcomes associated with diabetes as the patients would have likely been in the hospital from a condition related to their diabetes.

Code 
#creating dummy variables for the categorical variables in discharge disposition
expired = pd.get_dummies(nomedData1['discharge_disposition_id'])
Code 
nomedData1['Expired in Hospital'] = expired['Expired in Hospital']
nomedData1['Expired out of Hospital'] = expired['Expired out of Hospital']
Code 
# getting the proportion of expiration for patients outside of skilled nusing facilities
nomedData1[nomedData1['admission_source_id'] != 'Skilled Nursing Facility Transfer']['Expired in Hospital'].mean()
0.015865465608308312
Code 
# getting the proportion of expiration for patients from skilled nusing facilities
nomedData1[nomedData1['admission_source_id'] == 'Skilled Nursing Facility Transfer']['Expired in Hospital'].mean()
0.047953216374269005
Code 
#dividing the proportion of expiration for patients from skilled nursing facilities by the proportion of expiration for patients from other sources
0.047953216374269005 / 0.015593191434935996
3.075266315709529
Code 
# sns.set(font_scale = 1)
sns.barplot(data=nomedData1, x='admission_source_id', y='Expired in Hospital',
            palette=['#728FCE', '#9E7BFF', '#FC6C85', '#90EE90', '#F4A460'])
plt.xticks(rotation=50, ha='right')
plt.ylabel('Expiration in Hospital')
plt.xlabel('Admission Source')
plt.suptitle('Proportion of Expiration Across Admission Sources')
Text(0.5, 0.98, 'Proportion of Expiration Across Admission Sources')

Patients from skilled nursing facility had a proportion of patient expiration that was approximately three times higher than the average expiration proportion from other sources.

The graph was then visualized by age to ensure that age was not a confounding variable. Observations were filtered out if there were 10 or less observations by age across these admission categories to avoid misleading data.

Code 
# filtering the data to exclude observations with less than ten total observartions by age and admission sources
filtered_data = nomedData1.groupby(['age', 'admission_source_id']).filter(lambda x: len(x) > 10)
Code 
# sns.set(font_scale = 1)
sns.barplot(data=filtered_data, x='admission_source_id', y='Expired in Hospital', hue='age', ci=None)
plt.xticks(rotation=50, ha='right')

plt.xlabel('Admission Source')
plt.suptitle('Proportion of Expiration Across Admission Sources')
plt.legend(title='Age Groups', loc='lower right', bbox_to_anchor=(1.25, 0));

Patients from skilled nursing facilities had higher proportions of patient expiration across most age groups, as well.

2.4 Analysis 4: Which drugs are prescribed the most and how might those drugs affect diabetes patients?

By <Jeffrey Yuan>

To determine the usage of drugs and the related outcomes of patients using each drug, two variables were determined to be used as outcome measures. The first outcome measure analyzed with each drug was the Glucose Levels of the patients, associated with the max_glu_serum, and the second variable analyzed was the time till readmission for each patient.

In the dataset from diabetic patients in 130 hospitals from 1999 to 2008 there were a total of 23 drugs used.

Code 

drug_columns = [
    'metformin', 'repaglinide', 'nateglinide', 'chlorpropamide',
    'glimepiride', 'acetohexamide', 'glipizide', 'glyburide', 'tolbutamide',
    'pioglitazone', 'rosiglitazone', 'acarbose', 'miglitol', 'troglitazone',
    'tolazamide', 'examide', 'citoglipton', 'insulin', 'glyburide-metformin',
    'glipizide-metformin', 'glimepiride-pioglitazone', 'metformin-rosiglitazone',
    'metformin-pioglitazone'
]
print(*drug_columns, sep=' ,')
metformin ,repaglinide ,nateglinide ,chlorpropamide ,glimepiride ,acetohexamide ,glipizide ,glyburide ,tolbutamide ,pioglitazone ,rosiglitazone ,acarbose ,miglitol ,troglitazone ,tolazamide ,examide ,citoglipton ,insulin ,glyburide-metformin ,glipizide-metformin ,glimepiride-pioglitazone ,metformin-rosiglitazone ,metformin-pioglitazone

To determine the total usage of each drug concerning glucose level, the values of glucose that were ‘None’ were mapped to NaN. The missing values were not imputed because a conclusion based on imputed data can affect downstream conclusions, and inaccurate imputation of glucose levels may lead to incorrect findings in clinical studies and inappropriate medical decisions. The subset of the data with glucose levels was taken for analysis. The total number of patients who used each drug and the corresponding distribution of glucose levels were visualized. Glucose levels were binned into normal levels, levels greater than 200, and levels greater than 300 in the data.

Code 
# Subsetting data where there are glucose values
glucose = diabeticDataDf[~diabeticDataDf.max_glu_serum.isnull()]
# plot of the number of occurances of each drug by glucose level
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
# subsetting and formatting data for ploting
df_melted_glucose = pd.melt(glucose, id_vars=['max_glu_serum'], value_vars=drug_columns)
df_melted_glucose = df_melted_glucose[df_melted_glucose['value'] != 'No']
sns.countplot(data=df_melted_glucose, x='variable', hue='max_glu_serum', order=drug_columns,
              hue_order=['Norm', '>200', '>300'])
plt.title('Counts of Drug Treatments by Glucose Levels')
plt.xlabel('Drug')
plt.ylabel('Count')
plt.legend(title='Max Glucose Serum Test Result', loc='upper left')
plt.xticks(ticks=range(len(drug_columns)), labels=[drug.capitalize() for drug in drug_columns], rotation=45, ha='right')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The six most common drugs in data are metformin, glipizide, glyburide, pioglitazone, rosiglitazone, and insulin. The total number of patients who use insulin, the most common drug, is over four times more than the second, metformin. The total number of patients who use insulin is also greater than those who use any other drug. The distribution of each of the six most common drugs and the corresponding distribution of glucose levels were visualized for clarity.

Code 
# Subsetting columns of 6 drugs of interest
drugs_of_interest_columns = ['metformin', 'glipizide', 'glyburide', 'pioglitazone', 'rosiglitazone', 'insulin']
# plot of the number of occurances of each of the 6 most common drugs by glucose level
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
# Subsetting and formatting data for plotting
df_melted_glucose_interest = pd.melt(glucose, id_vars=['max_glu_serum'], value_vars=drugs_of_interest_columns)
df_melted_glucose_interest = df_melted_glucose_interest[df_melted_glucose_interest['value'] != 'No']
# plotting distribution of glucose levels
sns.countplot(data=df_melted_glucose_interest, x='variable', hue='max_glu_serum', order=drugs_of_interest_columns,
              hue_order=['Norm', '>200', '>300'])
plt.title('Counts of Select Drug Treatments by Glucose Levels')
plt.xlabel('Drug')
plt.ylabel('Count')
plt.legend(title='Max Glucose Serum Test Result', loc='upper left')
plt.xticks(ticks=range(len(drugs_of_interest_columns)),
           labels=[drug.capitalize() for drug in drugs_of_interest_columns], ha='center')
plt.show()

The effectiveness of managing glucose levels was analyzed by finding the proportion of patients in each binned glucose level and visualizing the data.

Code 
# Calculate the proportions of glucose levels for each drug
proportion_data = df_melted_glucose_interest.groupby(['variable', 'max_glu_serum']).size().unstack()
proportion_data = proportion_data.divide(proportion_data.sum(axis=1), axis=0)
# Plotting proportion data
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
# Settig the bottom of the bars
bottom = np.zeros(len(proportion_data))
# Iterate over each glucose level
for glu_level in ['Norm', '>200', '>300']:
    plt.bar(
        proportion_data.index,
        proportion_data[glu_level],
        bottom=bottom,
        label=glu_level
    )
    bottom += proportion_data[glu_level].values
plt.title('Proportions of Select Drug Treatments by Glucose Levels')
plt.xlabel('Drug')
plt.ylabel('Proportion')
plt.xticks(ticks=range(len(proportion_data.index)), labels=[drug.capitalize() for drug in proportion_data.index],
           ha='center')
plt.legend(title='Max Glucose Serum Test Result', bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1))
plt.show()

The proportion of patients for each drug who had glucose levels >300 is the highest in insulin at 30%. However, metformin had only 23% of patients with glucose levels>300. Insulin also had the lowest proportion of patients with normal glucose levels at 35%, while metformin had 45% of patients with normal glucose levels.

The top two most common drugs, insulin and metformin, were used to perform a case study on the clinical usage of each drug concerning a patient’s glucose level. For both drugs, the proportion of patients who kept a steady level of drug usage and increased prescription was visualized against the glucose level.

Code 
# Subsetting data for Graph of Insulin and Metformin usage based of glucose levels
administeredMeds = diabeticDataDf[
    (~diabeticDataDf.metformin.isin(['No', 'Down'])) & (~diabeticDataDf.insulin.isin(['No', 'Down']))]
# Finding propotion of insulin usage for all levels of diabetes progression in Insulin and Metformin
insulin = pd.crosstab(administeredMeds.max_glu_serum, administeredMeds.insulin, normalize='index')
insulin = insulin.reindex(['Norm', '>200', '>300'])
metformin = pd.crosstab(administeredMeds.max_glu_serum, administeredMeds.metformin, normalize='index')
metformin = metformin.reindex(['Norm', '>200', '>300'])
# Plotting data
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2)
fig.suptitle('Insulin and Metformin Usage by Glucose Level')
insulin.plot.bar(stacked=True, ax=ax1)
ax1.legend(title='Insulin', bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1))
ax1.set_xlabel('Glucose Level')
ax1.set_ylabel('Proportion')
ax1.set_xticklabels(ax1.get_xticklabels(), rotation=0)
metformin.plot.bar(stacked=True, ax=ax2)
ax2.legend(title='Metformin', bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1))
ax2.set_xlabel('Glucose Level');
ax2.set_ylabel('Proportion')
ax2.set_xticklabels(ax2.get_xticklabels(), rotation=0)
plt.tight_layout()

When a patient has worse levels of diabetes progression, the proportion of patients to receive a higher prescription of insulin is much higher than metformin. Of patients with glucose levels >300, 49% receive a higher prescription insulin. A 28% increase in patients with glucose levels >200. However, of patients on a metformin regimen, 15% receive increased metformin, only an 8% increase from patients with glucose levels >200. There is a 20% discrepancy in the increase of clinical insulin prescriptions compared to metformin.

The second outcome measure was readmission. Continuing with the six most common drugs found above, each drug’s proportion of patients in the binned readmission times was visualized. Readmission was binned into patients with no record of readmission, readmitted after 30 days, and readmitted within 30 days. Missing values were not imputed due to potentially false conclusions impacting clinical decision-making.

Code 
# Subsetting data for readmission analysis
readmit = diabeticDataDf.loc[diabeticDataDf['readmitted'] != 'None']
readmit['readmitted'].value_counts()
df_melted_re_interest = pd.melt(readmit, id_vars=['readmitted'], value_vars=drugs_of_interest_columns)
df_melted_re_interest = df_melted_re_interest[df_melted_re_interest['value'] != 'No']
# Calculateing the proportions of readmission for each drug
proportion_data = df_melted_re_interest.groupby(['variable', 'readmitted']).size().unstack().fillna(0)
proportion_data = proportion_data.divide(proportion_data.sum(axis=1), axis=0)
# Plotting data
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
# Settng the bottom of the bars
bottom = np.zeros(len(proportion_data))
# Iterate over each glucose level
for readmitted in ['NO', '>30', '<30']:
    plt.bar(
        proportion_data.index,
        proportion_data[readmitted],
        bottom=bottom,
        label=readmitted
    )
    bottom += proportion_data[readmitted].values
plt.title('Proportions of Select Drug Treatments by Readmittance')
plt.xlabel('Drug')
plt.ylabel('Proportion')
plt.xticks(ticks=range(len(proportion_data.index)), labels=[drug.capitalize() for drug in proportion_data.index],
           ha='center')
plt.legend(title='Readmittance Result', bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1))
plt.show()

There was not a larger difference in distribution of patients readmisson between all 6 of the most common drugs. There are ~52% of patients not readmitted, ~37% of patients readmitted after 30 days, and ~11% of patients who are readmitted within 30 days of their visit.
